concepts.name: Electric potential energy
concepts.statement: The electrostatic or Coulomb force is conservative, which means that the work done on a charge is independent of the path taken, exactly as for gravity in the absence of friction. When a force is conservative, it is possible to define a potential energy associated with the force, and it is usually easier to deal with the potential energy, because it depends only on position, than to calculate the work directly. The work done by a conservative force is the negative of the change in potential energy, so work done to accelerate a positive charge from rest is positive and results from a loss in PE.

concepts.name: Electric potential
concepts.statement: The electric potential is the potential energy per unit charge, $V = \text{PE}/q$. Since the work done by the field, and hence the change in potential energy, is proportional to the test charge, the dependence on the charge cancels and $V$ does not depend on $q$.

concepts.name: Potential difference
concepts.statement: The potential difference between points A and B is the change in potential energy of a charge moved from A to B, divided by the charge. Its unit, the joule per coulomb, is the volt, named after Alessandro Volta. Voltage is the common name for potential difference, and a voltage always means the potential difference between two points. Voltage is not the same as energy: a motorcycle battery and a car battery can both be 12 V, yet one stores much more energy than the other.

concepts.name: Finding energy from a potential difference
concepts.statement: The relationship between potential difference and electrical potential energy can be read either way: the potential difference is the change in potential energy per unit charge, and the change in potential energy is the charge times the potential difference. To find the energy a battery delivers, multiply the charge it moves by its voltage; to find the charge that moved, divide the energy by the voltage. The energies so found are absolute values, and the change in potential energy of a battery that loses energy is negative.

concepts.name: Charge motion and potential
concepts.statement: Downhill for the electron is uphill for a positive charge. A battery repels electrons from its negative terminal and attracts them to its positive terminal, so the negative charge moves from A to B through a change in potential of +12 V, and since the charge is negative, $\Delta\text{PE} = q\Delta V$ is negative and the potential energy of the battery has decreased. In terms of potential, the positive terminal is at a higher voltage than the negative, whichever sign of charge moves.

concepts.name: Zero of potential
concepts.statement: The point you choose to be zero volts is arbitrary, exactly as gravitational potential energy has an arbitrary zero such as sea level or a lecture hall floor. Every battery has two terminals, and its voltage is the potential difference between them; a potential quoted for a single point assumes a reference, usually infinity for a point charge or the ground for a meter, and it is the potential difference between two points that is of importance.

concepts.name: Electron volt
concepts.statement: On the submicroscopic scale the energy per particle is a tiny fraction of a joule, yet it can be enough to break up organic molecules and harm living tissue, so an energy unit on that scale is convenient. The electron volt is the energy a fundamental charge gains when accelerated through a potential difference of 1 V. An electron accelerated through 50 V gains 50 eV, and a doubly charged ion accelerated through 100 V gains 200 eV. The energy of the electron in electron volts is numerically the same as the voltage between the plates.

concepts.name: Conservation of energy for a charge
concepts.statement: The total energy of a system stays constant if no work or heat transfer adds to it or takes from it. For conservative forces such as the electrostatic force, conservation of energy says that mechanical energy, the sum of the kinetic energy and the potential energy, is a constant. A loss of PE of a charged particle becomes an increase in its KE, where PE is now the electric potential energy. As many times before, energy gives insight and makes problems easier than following the force.

concepts.name: Finding the speed of an accelerated charge
concepts.statement: With only conservative forces acting, all of the electrical potential energy of a charge accelerated from rest in a vacuum becomes kinetic energy, so $qV = mv^2/2$ gives the final speed. The large final speed of an electron confirms that the gravitational force is negligible. It also shows how easily small voltages accelerate electrons, because of their very small mass. Voltages much higher than 100 V produce speeds so great that relativistic effects matter.

forms.condition: a charge accelerated from rest, non-relativistic

concepts.name: Voltage and field between parallel plates
concepts.statement: In a uniform electric field the voltage between two points is the field strength times the distance between them along the field, $V_\text{AB} = Ed$, so the field is the voltage divided by the distance. The work the field does on a positive charge moved from the positive plate to the negative plate is both $qV_\text{AB}$ and $qEd$, and the charge cancels.

concepts.name: Potential as scalar, field as vector
concepts.statement: Either the potential difference or the electric field can describe any charge distribution. The potential difference is most closely tied to energy and is a scalar quantity with no direction, whereas the field is most closely related to force and is a vector with both magnitude and direction. The distinction matters when several charges act: voltages add as numbers, whereas fields add as vectors.

concepts.name: Units of the electric field
concepts.statement: The relation $E = V_\text{AB}/d$ implies that the units for electric field are volts per meter, and the units already known from the definition of the field are newtons per coulomb, so the two must be the same unit. Which of the two is written depends on whether the field is being read from a force or from a voltage; the force on a charge in Example 19.5 comes out in newtons because 1 V/m is 1 N/C.

concepts.name: Dielectric breakdown of air
concepts.statement: Dry air will support a maximum electric field strength of about $3.0 \times 10^6$ V/m. Above that value the field ionizes enough of the air to make it a conductor, allowing a discharge or spark that reduces the field. It therefore takes about 75 kV to make a spark jump across a 2.5 cm gap, which limits the voltages that can exist between conductors, such as those on a power transmission line. Points on a surface create greater fields than smooth surfaces and so spark at a smaller voltage, and humid air breaks down at a lower field strength than dry.

concepts.name: Field as potential gradient
concepts.statement: In general, whether or not the electric field is uniform, it points in the direction of decreasing potential, because the force on a positive charge points both along the field and toward lower potential. The magnitude of the field equals the rate of decrease of the potential with distance: the faster the potential decreases over distance, the greater the field. The minus sign says that the field points toward decreasing potential. For continually changing potentials the differences become infinitesimals, and you need differential calculus.

concepts.name: Electric potential of a point charge
concepts.statement: Point charges such as electrons are among the fundamental building blocks of matter, and spherical charge distributions create external fields exactly like a point charge, so the potential of a point charge is essential. Calculus gives the work needed to move a test charge from a large distance away to a distance $r$ from a point charge. With $W = -q\Delta V$, it shows that the potential is $kQ/r$, with zero potential at infinity. A negative value means the charge attracts a positive charge from a larger distance, since the potential there is lower than at larger distances.

forms.condition: point charge, with V = 0 at infinity

concepts.name: Potential versus field of a point charge
concepts.statement: The potential of a point charge decreases with distance, whereas the field of a point charge decreases with distance squared, since the field is the force per unit charge and Coulomb's law is an inverse square law. The two describe the same charge in two ways, and the difference in their fall-off is the difference between an energy per charge, which accumulates over the whole path in from infinity, and a force per charge, which acts at one point.

concepts.name: Superposition of potentials
concepts.statement: To find the voltage due to a combination of point charges, add the individual voltages as numbers. To find the total electric field, add the individual fields as vectors, taking magnitude and direction into account. This fits the fact that the potential goes with energy, a scalar, whereas the field goes with force, a vector. It makes the potential the easier quantity to work with when several charges are present.

concepts.name: Potential outside a charged sphere
concepts.statement: Charge on a metal sphere spreads out uniformly and produces a field like that of a point charge at its center. The potential on the surface and outside the sphere is therefore that of an equal point charge at the center, and you read the potential near the surface at the sphere's radius. That is why a Van de Graaff terminal's charge and radius set its voltage, and why isolated charge is difficult to store: a relatively small charge produces a large voltage.

concepts.name: Finding the potential energy of two charges
concepts.statement: To find the potential energy of a pair of point charges, take the potential of one at the position of the other and multiply by the second charge, since the potential is the potential energy per unit charge. The energy of a system of several charges is the sum over every pair. It is negative for unlike charges, which attract, and positive for like charges, which repel. Bringing like charges closer raises it, and bringing unlike charges closer lowers it.

concepts.name: Equipotential lines and equipotential surfaces
concepts.statement: Electric potentials can be represented pictorially, just as electric fields are drawn with field lines. Lines along which the electric potential is constant are called equipotential lines in two dimensions, or equipotential surfaces in three; the term equipotential is also used as a noun. The potential of a point charge is the same anywhere on a sphere of radius $r$ surrounding the charge, since it is given by $kQ/r$, so an equipotential surface of a point charge is a sphere and, in the plane, a circle. No work is required to move a charge anywhere along one of these lines, and work is needed to move a charge from one equipotential to another.

concepts.name: Equipotentials perpendicular to field lines
concepts.statement: Moving a charge along an equipotential takes no work, since the potential difference along it is zero, and work is zero only if the force is perpendicular to the motion. The force on a charge is in the direction of the field, so motion along an equipotential must be perpendicular to the field. With neither the charge, the field nor the distance zero, the cosine of the angle between them must vanish and the angle must be 90°. The rule holds in every case, and it lets you draw the equipotential lines from the field lines and the field lines from the equipotentials.

concepts.name: Conductor as an equipotential
concepts.statement: The electric field must be perpendicular to the surface of any conductor in static situations, and equipotentials are perpendicular to the field, so a conductor is an equipotential surface. There can be no voltage difference across the surface of a conductor, or charges would flow. Because a conductor is an equipotential, it can replace any equipotential surface. A charged spherical conductor can replace the point charge at the center of its equipotential spheres and leave the field and the potential outside unchanged. Conducting plates placed at the equipotential lines between two plates would maintain the same field.

concepts.name: Drawing equipotential lines
concepts.statement: Given the electric field lines, draw the equipotential lines perpendicular to them. Given the equipotential lines, as a voltmeter might measure them in a laboratory, draw the field lines perpendicular to the equipotentials. The potential is greatest near a positive charge and least near a negative one, so you can mark the direction of increasing potential too, and the field lines point from higher to lower potential.

concepts.name: Equipotential spacing and field strength
concepts.statement: Between two parallel conducting plates the equipotentials are evenly spaced and parallel, because the field is uniform and the potential falls at a constant rate across the gap. Where the field is stronger the potential changes faster with distance, so equipotentials drawn at equal steps of voltage crowd together; where it is weaker they spread apart. As the isolines of potential get closer together the field gets stronger, as a hill is steeper where the contours of gravitational potential crowd.

concepts.name: Capacitor
concepts.statement: A capacitor is a device that stores electric charge, with applications ranging from filtering static out of radio reception to energy storage in heart defibrillators. A commercial capacitor typically has two conducting parts close to one another but not touching, usually with an insulator between them. When you connect battery terminals to an initially uncharged capacitor, equal amounts of positive and negative charge separate onto its two plates. The capacitor remains neutral overall, but it is said to store a charge $Q$. The amount of charge it can store depends on the voltage applied and on its physical characteristics, such as its size.

concepts.name: Capacitance
concepts.statement: Capacitance is the amount of charge a capacitor stores per volt applied across it, $C = Q/V$. The greater the voltage applied to any capacitor, the greater the charge stored in it, and different capacitors store different charges for the same voltage. The unit of capacitance, the farad, is a coulomb per volt, a very large capacitance, and typical capacitors run from picofarads to millifarads.

forms.latex: E \propto Q, \quad V \propto E, \quad Q \propto V

concepts.name: Capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor
concepts.statement: A parallel plate capacitor is two identical conducting plates of area $A$ separated by a distance $d$. Like charges repel, unlike charges attract and the force between charges decreases with distance. The bigger the plates, the more charge they can store, because the charges can spread out more. The closer the plates, the greater the attraction of the opposite charges on them. The capacitance therefore grows with the area and shrinks with the separation, and these are the only two factors. The constant is the permittivity of free space, $8.85 \times 10^{-12}$ F/m, whose small value goes with the large size of the farad: a parallel plate capacitor must have a large area to approach a farad.

forms.condition: parallel plates separated by air or free space

concepts.name: Dielectric
concepts.statement: Making the separation smaller gives a larger capacitance, but then the maximum voltage must drop in proportion to avoid breakdown, since $E = V/d$. An important solution is to put an insulating material, called a dielectric, between the plates and make the separation as small as possible. The smaller separation raises the capacitance, and many insulators also withstand greater electric fields than air before breaking down. Water has a large dielectric constant but rarely serves as one, and humid air sparks at a lower voltage than dry.

concepts.name: Capacitance with a dielectric
concepts.statement: With a dielectric between the plates, the capacitance is greater than that of the same plates in vacuum by a factor $\kappa$, called the dielectric constant, which depends on the material. The constant for vacuum is exactly 1 and for air very close to it. Air-filled capacitors therefore act much like those with vacuum between their plates, except that air can become conductive if the field grows too great. Teflon's constant is 2.1, water's 80 and strontium titanate's 233. The same capacitor filled with Teflon has a greater capacitance and takes a much greater voltage, and so stores 42 times the charge.

concepts.name: Dielectric strength
concepts.statement: The dielectric strength of an insulating material is the maximum electric field strength above which it begins to break down and conduct. The field between parallel plates is the voltage over the separation, so the dielectric strength limits the voltage you can apply for a given plate separation. For 1.00 mm of air the limit is 3000 V, and for 1.00 mm of Teflon, whose strength is $60 \times 10^6$ V/m, it is 60,000 V.

concepts.name: Polarization of a dielectric
concepts.statement: Microscopically, a dielectric increases capacitance because it polarizes: the more easily its molecules polarize, the greater its dielectric constant. The Coulomb force between the closest ends of the polarized molecules and the charge on the plates is attractive and very strong, since they are very close together. It attracts more charge onto the plates than if the space were empty. Seen the other way, the field lines end on the surface charges of the dielectric, so fewer of them cross from one plate to the other. The field inside is less than in vacuum for the same charge, and so is the voltage $V = Ed$, and since $C = Q/V$ the capacitance is greater. The dielectric constant is the ratio of the field in vacuum to the field in the material, and it depends closely on the polarizability of the material. An atom polarizes because the external charges shift its electron cloud, and a polar molecule such as water carries an inherent separation of charge and so polarizes more readily.

concepts.name: Permittivity of free space
concepts.statement: The permittivity of free space is the constant $\varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}$ F/m that sets the capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor with a vacuum between its plates. Its small value is related to the large size of the farad.

concepts.name: Parallel plate capacitor
concepts.statement: A parallel plate capacitor is two identical conducting plates separated by a distance.

concepts.name: Equivalent capacitance
concepts.statement: Many applications connect several capacitors together, and the combination acts like a single equivalent capacitor. Its total capacitance depends both on the individual capacitors and on how they are connected. Two simple and common types of connection, series and parallel, give totals that are easy to calculate, and some more complicated connections reduce to combinations of the two.

concepts.name: Capacitance in series
concepts.statement: When you apply a voltage across a series connection of capacitors, opposite charges of magnitude $Q$ flow to either side of the originally uncharged combination. Conservation of charge requires equal-magnitude charges on the plates of each individual capacitor, since these originally neutral devices only separate charge. The voltages across the individual capacitors are $Q/C_1$, $Q/C_2$ and $Q/C_3$, and the total voltage is their sum. Writing the total as $Q/C_\text{S}$ and cancelling the charge gives the sum of reciprocals. The combination resembles a single capacitor with a larger effective plate separation than any of the individual ones, so the total capacitance in series is less than any of the individual capacitances.

concepts.name: Capacitance in parallel
concepts.statement: In a parallel connection the voltage across each capacitor equals that of the source, since a conductor connects each one directly to it and conductors are equipotentials. Each capacitor therefore holds the charge it would hold alone. The total charge is the sum of the individual charges, $C_\text{p}V = C_1V + C_2V + C_3V$, and cancelling the voltage makes the total capacitance in parallel simply the sum of the individual capacitances. The equivalent capacitor has an effectively larger plate area and so a larger capacitance.

concepts.name: Reducing series and parallel capacitors
concepts.statement: More complicated connections of capacitors can sometimes be combinations of series and parallel. To find the total capacitance, identify the series and parallel parts, compute their capacitances, and then find the total. For example, replace two capacitors in series by their series capacitance, then add it in parallel to a third. Working piece by piece until you reach a total works for larger combinations too.

concepts.name: Energy stored in a capacitor
concepts.statement: Energy stored in a capacitor is electrical potential energy and depends on the charge and voltage on the capacitor. Apply $\Delta\text{PE} = q\Delta V$ with care, because the capacitor starts with zero voltage and comes up to its full voltage as it charges. The average voltage during charging is half the final voltage, so the energy stored is half the product of the charge and the voltage, not the whole product. Since $Q = CV$, you can write the same energy in terms of any two of the charge, the voltage and the capacitance. The energy is in joules for a charge in coulombs, a voltage in volts and a capacitance in farads.

concepts.name: Average voltage while charging
concepts.statement: The first charge placed on a capacitor experiences a change in voltage of zero, since the capacitor has zero voltage when uncharged, and the final charge experiences the full voltage, since the capacitor now has its full voltage on it. The voltage rises in proportion to the charge, so the average voltage on the capacitor during the charging process is half the final voltage, and that is the voltage the full charge is to be taken as having passed through. This is why the energy is $QV/2$ and not $QV$.

concepts.name: Uses of capacitor energy
concepts.statement: A defibrillator stores its energy in a capacitor, and the operator can adjust it to fit the situation. A large charge delivered in a short burst to a set of paddles across a person's chest can stop the fast, irregular beating of cardiac or ventricular fibrillation and let the body's pacemaker resume normal patterns. Automated external defibrillators in many public places diagnose the patient's heart condition and apply the shock with appropriate energy and waveform. Less dramatically, capacitors in microelectronics supply energy while you change batteries, and they power the flash lamps on cameras.

concepts.name: Defibrillator
concepts.statement: A defibrillator is a machine that delivers an electrical shock to a heart attack victim's heart to restore its normal beating pattern. It stores its energy in a capacitor and releases it in a burst.
